meta.title: SpaceX is finally public — and the Artemis math just got a lot louder
meta.subtitle: An $85 billion IPO, a $20 billion bond two weeks later, and a $4 billion lunar lander contract that suddenly looks like a rounding error
meta.push_title: SpaceX is public: what it changes for Artemis
meta.push_body: An IPO, a $20B bond, and a 35% pullback in two weeks. The Artemis lander program now lives inside a public-market story.

body:
For twenty-four years SpaceX kept its books closed. On June 12 that ended. Shares of Space Exploration Technologies Corp., ticker SPCX, opened on Nasdaq at $150 after pricing at $135, peaked near $225, and have since rolled back to the $150-$160 range — a 35% swing in less than two weeks ([U.S. News](https://www.usnews.com/news/top-news/articles/2026-06-23/spacexs-wild-ride-is-just-getting-started)). The IPO raised $85.7 billion, the largest in market history ([BeBeez](https://bebeez.eu/2026/06/22/spacex-makes-its-nasdaq-debut-with-the-biggest-ipo-in-history/)). Ten days later the company filed plans for a $20 billion debt issuance, calling it the "Inaugural Bond Issuance" ([The Motley Fool](https://www.fool.com/investing/2026/06/22/why-rocket-lab-stock-keeps-dropping/)).

For the first time, NASA's lunar lander contractor is a publicly traded entity with quarterly earnings, an SEC paper trail, and a market that prices its prospects in real time. That changes how we read the Artemis program, not because the engineering changed — it didn't — but because the financial scaffolding behind it just became visible.

The S-1 prospectus itself is unusually direct about the Moon. It lists "passenger and cargo to Moon and Mars" alongside "lunar mining of rare materials," "lunar mass driver," and "lunar factories building AI compute satellites" as future markets that public investors are being asked to underwrite ([PJFP](https://pjfp.com/spacex-s1-ipo-filing-breakdown/)). The headline number embedded in the prospectus — a $28 trillion total addressable market — is meant to justify a $1.78 trillion debut valuation.

## The Artemis line item

SpaceX's Human Landing System contract — the one that puts astronauts on the lunar surface for Artemis III and Artemis IV — is currently worth $4.04 billion ([Fed-Spend](https://fed-spend.com/blog/spacex-government-contracts-nasa-dod-space-force)). NASA has paid roughly $2.67 billion of that so far, about 66 percent of the current award ([Douglas Messier on Substack](https://douglasmmessier.substack.com/p/spacexs-hls-contract-much-of-the)). A March 2026 NASA Office of Inspector General report put the potential ceiling at approximately $4.3 billion across both missions ([NASA OIG](https://oig.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/final-report-ig-26-004-nasas-management-of-the-human-landing-system-contracts.pdf)).

Stack that against the IPO proceeds. SpaceX raised $85.7 billion in a single transaction. The entire HLS program, including Artemis IV, is less than 5 percent of that. If you add the bond issuance, the company is on track to clear $100 billion in fresh capital inside a calendar month. The HLS contract — the contract on which the first American return to the Moon since 1972 depends — is now a rounding error inside SpaceX's capital structure.

That cuts two ways. On one hand, NASA's milestone payments are no longer the cash flow that keeps Starship moving. The program can absorb a delayed milestone or a contested invoice without changing SpaceX's solvency picture. On the other hand, public-market discipline now reaches into the lunar program. Every quarterly report will show how much R&D is going into Starship, how many launches happened, and how cleanly the company is hitting the milestones it sold investors.

## What the prospectus admits

The S-1 reads like an engineering memo with a finance gloss. SpaceX disclosed that it lost $2.6 billion from operations on $18.7 billion of revenue in 2025, and that operating losses kept piling up at the start of 2026 ([Associated Press via KRGV](https://www.krgv.com/news/spacex-reveals-plans-for-what-could-be-the-biggest-ever-initial-public-offering)). The company has burned more than $15 billion of cumulative R&D on Starship, including roughly $3 billion in 2025 alone ([PJFP](https://pjfp.com/spacex-s1-ipo-filing-breakdown/)).

The prospectus also acknowledges that Starship's payload-delivery debut to orbit is still expected in the second half of 2026, that the company is still preparing Flight 13, and that no propellant transfer demonstration has occurred yet at the scale Artemis requires ([Barchart](https://www.barchart.com/story/news/2584540/houston-we-have-liftoff-trading-the-spacex-ipo-with-loff)). That last item is not a footnote. NASA's mission architecture for Artemis III depends on transferring cryogenic propellant between Starships in low Earth orbit — a maneuver that no spacecraft has executed at that scale, and one the company itself flags as a milestone investors should track ([The Motley Fool](https://www.fool.com/investing/2026/06/23/spacex-ipo-passed-important-milestone/)).

## The valuation argument

Not everyone is convinced. Aswath Damodaran, the NYU finance professor known on Wall Street as the "dean of valuation," published an updated post-prospectus model in early June. He arrives at an enterprise value of $1.22 trillion and an equity value of approximately $1.3 trillion ([Aswath Damodaran](https://aswathdamodaran.blogspot.com/2026/06/a-weeks-ago-i-assessed-value-of-spacex.html)). Morningstar started coverage just before the IPO with a fair value of $780 billion, or about $63 per share ([BeBeez](https://bebeez.eu/2026/06/22/spacex-makes-its-nasdaq-debut-with-the-biggest-ipo-in-history/)).

At the IPO close on June 15, SpaceX's market capitalization sat above $2.5 trillion. By June 22, after the bond announcement, the company had shed roughly $400 billion in market value, with the stock down 16.4 percent to $154.60 on the day ([TechStock²](https://ts2.tech/en/category/nasdaqrklb/)). The spread between Damodaran's number and the market's number is more than $500 billion. That gap is, almost entirely, the value of Mars colonies, orbital AI compute, and lunar factories — none of which exist yet.

For Artemis watchers, the spread matters less than the volatility. SpaceX no longer needs NASA's money. It needs investors to keep believing in the long story. As long as they do, Starship development funding remains unconstrained. If the story breaks — through a failed flight, a deeper drawdown, or a credible competitor — SpaceX would face the same tension every public company faces: short-term margin discipline versus long-cycle moonshots.

## The Rocket Lab signal

The cleanest read on sector sentiment comes from how other space stocks behaved around the IPO. Rocket Lab fell 7.2 percent on the day SpaceX announced its bond ([The Motley Fool](https://www.fool.com/investing/2026/06/22/why-rocket-lab-stock-keeps-dropping/)). AST SpaceMobile dropped more than 10 percent on June 12 itself, as money rotated out of pure-plays to fund the SpaceX trade ([Prospero.Ai](https://prosperoai.substack.com/p/doubling-down-on-the-poor-mans-spacex)). Deutsche Bank downgraded ASTS to Hold the same week ([Intellectia](https://intellectia.ai/news/stock/space-sector-pullback-as-investors-reassess-risks)).

What that tells us: the entire space sector is now being priced relative to SpaceX. Every contract win or test flight by Rocket Lab, Blue Origin, or Sierra Space will be compared against SpaceX's progress on Starship and Starlink V3. The Artemis program — which deliberately maintained a competing lander track with Blue Origin's Blue Moon for Artemis V — is operating inside a market that increasingly assumes SpaceX wins by default.

## Five things to watch

The Motley Fool's milestone list for SPCX shareholders happens to overlap almost perfectly with the Artemis critical path ([The Motley Fool](https://www.fool.com/investing/2026/06/23/spacex-ipo-passed-important-milestone/)):

- Starship V3 debut. Carrying real payload to orbit in H2 2026. Without V3, there is no Artemis III lander.
- Orbital propellant transfer. NASA's plan requires it. SpaceX has not yet demonstrated it. Slip on this single item slips Artemis IV more than Artemis III, since Artemis III is now scheduled as a low-Earth-orbit docking mission ([El-Balad/AP](https://www.el-balad.com/16899040)).
- Starlink V3 deployment on Starship. The first revenue case that proves V3 reusability. Investors will treat this as a proxy for Artemis hardware maturity.
- A successful Starship launch from Florida. The Federal Aviation Administration has completed the environmental review for LC-39A, but SpaceX still needs the final launch license. A second launch site reduces single-point-of-failure risk for both Starlink and Artemis.
- Flight 13 of Starship, currently slated for June 29 ([U.S. News](https://www.usnews.com/news/top-news/articles/2026-06-23/spacexs-wild-ride-is-just-getting-started)).

If any of those slip materially, SpaceX's stock will move. If the stock moves enough, the financing case for the rest of the moonshot story gets harder.

## Where this leaves us

The Artemis program has always been at least partly a story about money: cost-plus versus fixed-price, $20 billion saved by selecting SpaceX over Blue Origin in 2021, audit reports on milestone payments, and quiet contract modifications. None of that changes. What changes is that the financial story now plays out in public, in real time, and on a much larger stage.

For the next twelve months, the most useful Artemis watchlist is no longer just SLS stacking photos and HLS milestone announcements. It is also a ticker. SPCX is now part of the program's risk model whether NASA wants it there or not.
